title: India's Tourism Boom Is Real — and Lopsided: 4.29 Billion Domestic Visits, but Growth Concentrated in a Few Markets
excerpt: Domestic tourist visits jumped 45.6% to about 4.29 billion in 2025, yet hotel occupancy runs at 75% in tier-one cities against 57% in tier-three markets, and a 161,000-room pipeline is betting on closing that gap.
body:
• India recorded approximately 4.29 billion domestic tourist visits in 2025, up 45.6% from 2.95 billion in 2024, according to Ministry of Tourism data.
  • The hotel market underneath that boom is uneven: occupancy averaged 75% in tier-one cities and 57% in tier-three cities in 2025/26, and about one in four surveyed hotels saw revenue per available room decline.
  • Developers are betting heavily on the gap closing: a pipeline of about 161,000 branded rooms over five years — roughly 77% of existing branded inventory — with almost 80% of it outside tier-one markets.
  • How Indians actually travel explains the opportunity: buses account for 55.8% of household overnight journeys and railways 17.7%, per the first National Household Travel Survey.

India's tourism growth is not in doubt. Its distribution is. Domestic tourist visits reached approximately 4.29 billion in 2025 — counting visits, not individual travellers — up 45.6% from 2.95 billion a year earlier, according to Ministry of Tourism figures compiled by Itinerary Master's analysis of the data. The travel and tourism sector contributed 5.22% of India's GDP and supported about 8.46 crore jobs in 2023-24.

The uneven part, in hotel numbers

The Hotelivate-Savills 2026 Indian Hospitality Trends & Opportunities report, covering 2,168 hotels and 209,180 branded rooms, puts national occupancy at 68.1% in 2025/26, with average daily rates up 6.4% to Rs 8,962 and revenue per available room (RevPAR) up 6.2% to Rs 6,099, Hotel Report's summary of the study said.

Underneath the averages, the markets diverge. Bengaluru and Hyderabad led RevPAR growth among the 20 major markets, at 14.8% and 13.2%. Occupancy averaged 75% in tier-one cities but 57% in tier-three cities, and roughly one in four hotels in the survey recorded a RevPAR decline. Udaipur had the highest average room rate among the 20 major markets, alongside occupancy of about 58% — premium pricing on a thin base.

The pipeline is a bet on smaller cities

Developers have placed their chips on the gap. The five-year branded hotel pipeline has reached about 161,000 rooms — equivalent to roughly 77% of the country's existing branded inventory — with nearly 117,000 rooms already in active development. Almost 80% of the proposed rooms are outside tier-one markets, and close to half are planned for tier-three destinations: pilgrimage and regional cities such as Tirupati and Varanasi have proposed pipelines equivalent to several times their existing branded supply.

That is the "huge room for boom" in concrete terms: India has roughly one branded hotel room for every 3,000 people, a ratio industry executives cite as evidence of structural undersupply. It is also the risk. A tier-three city can record large visitor volumes while most journeys remain short pilgrimage or family trips that do not convert into room nights at the rates a new hotel needs.

How India actually travels

The first National Household Travel Survey, conducted between July 2025 and June 2026 across 492,023 households, found buses carried 55.8% of household overnight journeys and railways 17.7% — together nearly three-quarters. Air travel, which dominates the industry's attention, is a small share of how the country actually moves.

The government's response targets discovery as much as capacity. On September 27, 2026, the Ministry of Tourism launched the National Digital Tourism Stack and the National Mission for Alternative Destinations under the Dekho Apna Desh 2.0 campaign, aimed at spreading visitors beyond the destinations that already dominate itineraries. Whether 161,000 new rooms fill will depend less on the national growth rate — which is spectacular — than on whether those two programmes can move demand to the cities where the rooms are being built.
nri_angle: For diaspora travellers, the numbers explain the split experience of India trips: polished capacity in the big metros, thinner hotel supply in the smaller cities family visits actually go to.
author: Diaspora Desk
